title: Engine overheating
metaDesc: Temperature gauge high or temp warning light on? Answer a few quick questions to see the likely cause, whether to stop driving, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: my car is overheating what do i do
intro: An overheating engine is one of the few problems where minutes matter. Driving while it's in the red can warp or crack expensive engine parts. Answer the questions below to see how urgent it is, the likely causes, and what to check once the engine has cooled.
safety: If the gauge is in the red, a red temperature light is on, or steam is coming from under the hood, pull over safely and turn the engine off.
Never open the radiator cap or coolant tank cap on a hot engine. Hot coolant under pressure can spray out and cause serious burns.
If the oil pressure light comes on too, or the engine starts knocking, shut it off right away.
If you see flames or smoke with a burning smell, get everyone out and away from the car and call for help.

q_how_hot.q: How hot is it running right now (or the last time it happened)?
q_how_hot.help: On most cars the needle sits near the middle once the engine is warm. Some cars have only a light: red usually means hot, blue means still cold.

opts.a: The gauge is in the red, a red temperature light or message is on, or there's steam from under the hood
Higher than normal, but not in the red
It ran hot earlier but is back to normal now
I'm not sure

q_signs.q: Do you notice any of these?

opts.a: Steam, or a sweet, syrupy smell from under the hood
A temperature warning light or message on the dash
None of these. The gauge just looks higher than usual
I'm not sure

q_coolant_level.q: Once the engine has cooled for at least 30 minutes, where is the coolant level in the see-through overflow tank?
q_coolant_level.help: The overflow tank is a plastic bottle near the radiator with MIN and MAX (or COLD and FULL) marks. Only check it when the engine is cold, and don't open the radiator cap itself.

opts.a: Below the MIN mark, or the tank is empty
Between MIN and MAX
I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_leak_signs.q: Do you see any clues about where the coolant is going?
q_leak_signs.help: Coolant is usually green, orange, pink, blue or yellow, feels slightly slimy, and smells sweet.

opts.a: Drips or a puddle under the front of the car, or wet, crusty spots on hoses or the radiator
Thick white exhaust smoke that smells sweet, milky oil on the dipstick, or bubbles in the coolant tank
No leak I can see anywhere
I'm not sure

q_when.q: The coolant is full. When does it run hot?

opts.a: Only when idling or in slow traffic. It cools down once I'm moving
Mostly at highway speed, climbing hills or towing
It climbs within a few minutes of starting, or the heater blows cold while the gauge is high
The needle jumps around, but the heater stays hot and there's no steam or smell
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be overheating. Stop as soon as it's safe
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Then call for a tow or a mobile mechanic rather than restarting it.
if: If you're stuck in traffic and can't pull over yet, turn the A/C off and the heater on full hot with the fan on high. This pulls some heat away from the engine until you can stop.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, shut it off immediately, even before you reach the roadside.
If coolant is pouring out or you see flames or heavy smoke, get everyone away from the car.
If the check engine light starts flashing, the engine may be misfiring from the heat. Turn it off.
result.why: A gauge in the red or steam from the engine usually means it can no longer get rid of heat fast enough. Every extra minute of running can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket, turning a simple hose or fan repair into a major engine repair.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: Steam, a sweet smell, a puddle under the front of the car, or an empty overflow tank once cool.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: It got hot while idling or in traffic, not at highway speed.
causes.against: If it overheated at steady highway speed, the fan matters much less.

causes.name: Water pump, thermostat or burst hose
causes.clues: It got hot quickly, the heater blew cold, or there was a sudden cloud of steam.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke, or bubbles in the coolant tank.

you: Once fully cool, look at the overflow tank level and under the car for drips.
Note what you saw: steam, smells, smoke and how fast the gauge rose. It helps the shop.
shop: Cooling fan and fan relay test
Combustion gas (block) test for a head gasket leak

result.title: Check the coolant level before driving again
result.now: Don't drive it again until you've checked the coolant. With the engine fully cold, look at the overflow tank. If it's below MIN, top it up to the MAX line with the coolant type listed in your owner's manual, and have the cooling system checked before relying on the car.
if: If the tank was empty or very low, coolant is escaping somewhere. Have the leak found before driving, because it will usually overheat again.
If the level is between MIN and MAX, come back and answer the questions again with that. The cause is more likely a fan, thermostat or pump.
If you see a puddle, milky oil or sweet-smelling white exhaust smoke, don't drive it. Have it towed or checked where it is.
If the gauge ever reaches the red, a red temperature light comes on or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Low coolant is one of the most common reasons an engine runs hot, and it's easy to check safely once the engine is cold. The level tells you whether you're dealing with a leak or a problem with the fan, thermostat or pump.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The tank is below MIN, or you've had to top it up before.
causes.against: A full tank makes this less likely, though air in the system can still cause trouble.

causes.name: Cooling fan problem
causes.clues: It runs hot in traffic and cools down when moving.

causes.name: Thermostat or water pump
causes.clues: The coolant is full but it still heats up quickly.

you: Check the overflow tank level with the engine cold.
Look under the front of the car for drips after it's been parked.
Watch whether the radiator fan runs once the engine is warm and idling.
shop: Code scan for temperature sensor and fan codes

result.title: Coolant may be leaking out, so the engine can't stay cool
result.now: Don't drive it until the leak has been checked. Once the engine is cold you can top up the overflow tank to MAX with the right coolant, but since it has already run hot, have a mobile mechanic look at it or have it towed.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a red temperature light comes on or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off right away.
If coolant is pouring out or the tank empties quickly, don't start the engine again.
If the oil looks milky or there's sweet-smelling white exhaust smoke, mention it. It may point to an internal leak.
Once a shop has found the leak, they can tell you whether it's OK to drive the car to have it repaired.
result.why: The cooling system is sealed, so coolant usually only goes down when it's escaping somewhere. Once enough is lost, the engine can't move heat to the radiator and the temperature climbs. Fixing the leak early often means a hose, clamp or radiator repair rather than engine damage. A pressure test usually shows where it's coming from.

causes.name: Leaking radiator hose or clamp
causes.clues: Wet or crusty spots at hose ends, or a hose that feels soft and swollen.

causes.name: Leaking radiator
causes.clues: Drips from the very front of the car, or crusty colored deposits on the radiator.

causes.name: Leaking water pump
causes.clues: Drips or a crusty trail near the engine-belt end of the engine.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Coolant residue around the cap, or the tank overflows when hot.

you: Put a piece of cardboard under the engine overnight to see where it drips.
Look for wet or crusty colored deposits on hoses, the radiator and around the engine.

result.title: Possible head gasket leak: coolant may be getting into the engine
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic test it.
if: If a test rules out a head gasket, a leaking intake gasket or EGR or oil cooler (on some engines) can cause similar signs, and those are usually less serious.
If the oil looks milky, don't start the engine at all. Coolant mixed into oil can quickly damage the bearings.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, don't restart it.
result.why: Sweet-smelling white exhaust smoke, milky oil, or bubbles in the coolant tank all suggest coolant and combustion gases are mixing inside the engine. Driving on it can spread the damage, but catching it early often keeps the repair smaller. A shop will usually run a combustion gas test and a pressure test before recommending head work.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Bubbles in the coolant tank while running, white sweet-smelling exhaust, or coolant loss with no leak.

causes.name: Warped or cracked cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine was badly overheated recently.

causes.name: Leaking oil cooler or intake gasket
causes.clues: Milky oil without white exhaust smoke, on engines that have these parts.

you: With the engine off and cool, check the dipstick and under the oil filler cap for a milky, light-brown sludge.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test on the coolant

result.title: Coolant may be escaping somewhere you can't see
result.now: Don't drive it until the cooling system has been pressure-tested. Not seeing a leak doesn't mean the coolant is safe to top up and forget. Once the engine is cold you can top up the tank, but have a mobile mechanic test it or have it towed.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a red temperature light comes on or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you notice white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or milky oil, don't start the engine. That can point to an internal leak.
If the windows fog up or the passenger floor is damp, the heater core is a possible source. Mention it to the shop.
Once a shop has found where the coolant is going, they can tell you whether it's OK to drive the car to have it repaired.
result.why: Some leaks only happen when the system is hot and under pressure, and the coolant evaporates before it can drip. Others leak inside the car or inside the engine. A pressure test usually shows where it's going.

causes.name: Small leak that evaporates when hot
causes.clues: A sweet smell after driving, or crusty colored deposits on hoses or the water pump.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, foggy windows, or a damp passenger floor.

causes.name: Internal leak (head gasket)
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke, milky oil, or bubbles in the coolant tank.
causes.against: If the oil and exhaust look normal, this is less likely.

you: Mark the coolant level and check how fast it drops.
Feel the passenger-side carpet for dampness.
Check the oil for a milky look.

result.title: The radiator fan may not be doing its job
result.now: Until the cooling fan has been checked, only drive if you can avoid idling and stop-and-go traffic, and watch the temperature gauge the whole time. Get it checked within the next few days.
if: If the gauge rises in traffic, turn the A/C off and the heater on full hot, and pull over and switch off before it reaches the red.
If the fan never spins at all with the engine hot, don't drive it in any traffic until it's fixed.
If you see steam or smell hot coolant, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: At speed, air rushes through the radiator by itself. When you're stopped, the fan has to pull that air through. Running hot only in traffic and cooling off once moving is a classic sign that the fan isn't working properly. A shop will usually check the fuse, relay and wiring before replacing the fan motor.

causes.name: Failed electric fan motor
causes.clues: The fan doesn't spin even with the engine hot or the A/C on.

causes.name: Fan relay, fuse or wiring fault
causes.clues: The fan works sometimes, or a check engine light is on.

causes.name: Worn fan clutch (belt-driven fans)
causes.clues: Common on trucks and older rear-wheel-drive cars. The fan spins freely by hand with the engine off and cold.

you: With the engine warm and idling and the A/C on, see whether the radiator fan is spinning. Keep hands and clothing clear, because electric fans can start on their own.
shop: Cooling fan motor and relay test
Code scan for fan circuit codes

result.title: The radiator or coolant flow may not be keeping up under load
result.now: Avoid towing, long climbs and high speeds, and get the cooling system checked within the next few days.
if: If the gauge climbs above its normal spot, ease off, and pull over and turn the engine off before it reaches the red.
If the front of the radiator is packed with leaves, bugs or dirt, gently rinsing it with a garden hose at low pressure (not a pressure washer) may help.
If you see steam, smell hot coolant or a red temperature light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Under heavy load the engine makes the most heat, so a cooling system that's only partly working shows up first on hills, on the highway, or when towing. Common culprits restrict how much coolant flows or how much heat the radiator can release.

causes.name: Partly clogged radiator
causes.clues: An older radiator, coolant that hasn't been changed in years, or debris blocking the front.

causes.name: Thermostat not opening fully
causes.clues: The gauge rises slowly under load but drops when you ease off.

causes.name: Weak water pump
causes.clues: A whine or grinding noise near the belt, or a coolant trail from the pump.

you: Look at the front of the radiator through the grille for debris.
Note when the gauge rises: hills, speed or towing.

result.title: Coolant may not be circulating: thermostat, water pump or trapped air
result.now: Don't drive it until it's checked. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If coolant was recently changed or added, trapped air may be the cause. A shop can bleed the air out.
If you hear grinding or see coolant dripping near the engine belt, the water pump may have failed. Mention it to the shop.
result.why: If the engine heats up within minutes, or the heater blows cold while the gauge is high, hot coolant isn't moving through the engine and heater the way it should. That will overheat the engine again on almost any drive.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes.clues: The gauge rises quickly and the upper radiator hose stays cool while the engine is hot.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: A grinding or whining noise, or coolant leaking from near the belt.

causes.name: Air trapped in the cooling system
causes.clues: It started after coolant work, or you hear gurgling behind the dash.

you: Note whether the problem started right after any coolant service or repair.
shop: Hose temperature comparison with an infrared thermometer

result.title: It may be a faulty temperature sensor or gauge, not real overheating
result.now: Get the temperature sensor and gauge checked within the next few days. Until a shop confirms the engine isn't really overheating, treat any high reading as real: watch for steam, smells or a heater that turns cold, and pull over if the needle reaches the red.
if: If a temperature warning light comes on, you see steam, or the heater suddenly blows cold, treat it as real overheating. Pull over and turn the engine off.
If the check engine light is on, a code scan can quickly point to the sensor.
result.why: A real overheating engine usually shows other signs, like steam, a sweet smell or a heater that turns cold. A needle that jumps around while everything else seems normal often means the sensor or its wiring is sending a bad signal. A shop can compare it with the real temperature.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The needle jumps suddenly, or a check engine light is on.

causes.name: Loose or corroded sensor wiring
causes.clues: It changes over bumps or in wet weather.

causes.name: Low coolant around the sensor
causes.clues: The overflow tank is low, which can leave the sensor in an air pocket.
causes.against: If the coolant is full, this is less likely.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Note whether the heater stays hot when the needle reads high.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data
Infrared temperature check of the engine

result.title: Treat it as possible overheating until it's checked
result.now: Before driving again, check the coolant level with the engine cold. Then have the cooling system checked within the next few days.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature light comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the coolant tank is low, have the cooling system checked before driving. Low coolant usually means a leak, even if you can't see one.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over and turn it off right away.
result.why: Without clear signs it's hard to say whether the engine is truly overheating. Checking the coolant and getting a quick cooling system test is the safest way to avoid serious engine damage.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: One of the most common causes of running hot.

causes.name: Cooling fan problem
causes.clues: It runs hotter in traffic.

causes.name: Thermostat or sensor fault
causes.clues: The gauge moves oddly or rises quickly.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Take a photo of the gauge when it reads high, so the shop knows what you saw.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data
